Abstract 
37 
The efficient extraction of essential oils (EOs), particularly volatile compounds, from medicinal, 
38 
aromatic, or oil-rich crop plants using supercritical carbon dioxide extraction (scCO2) is crucial for 
39 
industries such as pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and food. However, optimizing this process presents 
40 
challenges due to the intricate molecular diversity of the compounds and the complex interplay of 
41 
scCO2 parameters. To address these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid predictive framework 
42 
that combines deep learning and machine learning, utilizing 694 scCO2 experimental data points 
43 
sourced from the literature across 21 plant species. Four major molecular compounds per plant were 
44 
selected as input features, alongside key process parameters, including temperature, pressure, 
45 
extraction time, co-solvent ratio, and CO2 flow rate. Morgan fingerprints were computed for these 
46 
compounds, and a convolutional neural network (CNN) was utilized to extract their high-level 
47 
representations into compact vectors. These vectors were integrated with normalized process 
48 
parameters and fed into a CNN-Multilayer Perceptron (CNN-MLP) hybrid architecture. 
49 
Performance was compared with Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest (RF), Gaussian 
50 
Process Regression (GPR), and XGBoost, all optimized using OPTUNA. The CNN-MLP achieved 
51 
the best performance, with an R2 of 0.974 and a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 1.431 on the 
52 
test set. A paired t-test (p = 0.810) and Bland–Altman analysis (mean difference: 9.35%) confirmed 
53 
the model's robustness. To further assess generalizability, external validations were conducted using 
54 
unseen experimental conditions. The CNN-MLP was tested on three extraction profiles and 
55 
demonstrated strong predictive performance, with Pearson correlations ranging from 0.95 to 0.98.

1. 
Introduction 
66 
Since the COVID-19 pandemic, global interest in natural health products and alternative 
67 
medicines has surged dramatically. In the United States alone, approximately 80% of adults report 
68 
using medicinal plants to improve their health, reflecting a broader shift toward sustainable and 
69 
holistic solutions (US Pharmacopeia, 2023). This trend is mirrored in the rapid expansion of the 
70 
global medicinal plant market, which was valued at $146.6 billion in 2023 and is projected to reach 
71 
$248.6 billion by 2030, with a compound annual growth rate of 6.8% [1]. Central to this growth are 
72 
EOs and volatile compounds extracted from medicinal plants, which are prized for their bioactive 
73 
properties and applications across pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, food, and aromatherapy [2]. 
74 
Supercritical Fluid Extraction (SFE) has emerged as a gold-standard technique for isolating 
75 
various compounds, offering advantages such as tunable selectivity, environmental sustainability, 
76 
and solvent-free operation [3,4]. By utilizing supercritical carbon dioxide, SFE allows for precise 
77 
control over extraction parameters (e.g., temperature and pressure), resulting in oils with 
78 
customized chemical profiles [5].  However, optimizing SFE remains a challenge due to the 
79 
complex interplay between the molecular diversity of plant constituents (e.g., terpenes and 
80 
phenolics) and the multifaceted nature of process conditions (e.g., temperature and pressure). 
81 
Traditional models often oversimplify these complexities, overlooking chemical heterogeneity and 
82 
failing to integrate molecular data with engineering parameters [6]. 
83 
This gap underscores the potential of cheminformatics, a discipline that integrates 
84 
computational analysis with chemical data [7,8]. Molecular fingerprints, which are numerical 
85 
representations of molecular structures, have proven particularly valuable for tasks such as 
86 
compound identification, property prediction, and extraction modeling [9,10]. In SFE, these 
87 
fingerprints can encode critical chemical features of plant constituents, facilitating data-driven 
88 
connections between molecular attributes and extraction outcomes [11]. 
89 
Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) present promising 
90 
solutions [12,13]. While traditional ML models, such as RF and XGBoost, excel in regression tasks, 
91 
they often struggle with high-dimensional data, such as molecular fingerprints [14–16]. CNNs, 
92 
which are widely used in image recognition, are particularly well-suited for distilling spatial 
93 
hierarchies from such data, thereby extracting latent features that enhance predictive power [17,18]. 
94 
Hybrid architectures, such as CNN-Multilayer Perceptron (CNN-MLP) frameworks, further 
95 
facilitate the integration of heterogeneous inputs, including chemical fingerprints and process 
96 
parameters, a capability that remains underexplored in the optimization of SFE processes [19]. 
97 
In this study, we propose a novel hybrid modeling approach that integrates molecular and 
98 
engineering perspectives to optimize SFE. A comprehensive dataset of SCO2 experiments was 
99 


3 
 
compiled across various plant species, focusing on the most abundant volatile compounds in each 
100 
species. Morgan molecular fingerprints were generated for these compounds, and a custom 
101 
convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture processed these fingerprints to extract latent 
102 
chemical features. These features were combined with critical supercritical carbon dioxide (SCO2) 
103 
extraction process parameters, including temperature, pressure, extraction time, co-solvent, and 
104 
flow rate, and were subsequently input into a multilayer perceptron (MLP) network. For 
105 
comparative analysis, traditional ML models, such as SVR, RF, GPR, and XGBoost, were trained 
106 
on the same hybrid dataset, with hyperparameters optimized using the OPTUNA framework. This 
107 
work aims to demonstrate how the integration of chemoinformatics and DL can enhance predictive 
108 
modeling in SFE, paving the way for data-driven, precision extraction protocols.

2.1. 
Dataset composition and process parameter definitions 
111 
SFE is an efficient separation technique that utilizes supercritical carbon dioxide (CO2), 
112 
which is non-toxic, non-flammable, and environmentally friendly, to selectively extract bioactive 
113 
compounds from complex plant matrices. Its tunable properties allow for the gentle recovery of 
114 
heat-sensitive molecules, such as EOs and antioxidants, without causing thermal degradation [20]. 
115 
A comprehensive dataset was curated to develop a robust predictive model for supercritical 
116 
CO2 (scCO2) extraction yield (in % w/w). The dataset comprises 694 experimental observations 
117 
derived from 21 plant species with diverse industrial applications (see Table S1). Each data point 
118 
represents a unique combination of operational conditions and plant-specific characteristics. The 
119 
selected species span multiple application domains, including pharmaceutical (e.g., Artemisia 
120 
annua), cosmetic (e.g., Rosmarinus officinalis), and food-related (e.g., Moringa oleifera) uses. 
121 
 
For each species, the four most abundant volatile or bioactive compounds were identified 
122 
based on published gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) profiles. These compounds 
123 
were encoded as 1024-bit Morgan molecular fingerprints using RDKit, derived from their canonical 
124 
Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) representations. This molecular encoding 
125 
captures the chemical identity of the target analytes, thereby enhancing the specificity of the model 
126 
across botanically diverse samples.

2.2. 
Statistical analysis and model evaluation criteria 
149 
To analyze the data, several key descriptive statistics were calculated, including the minimum, 
150 
maximum, standard deviation (STD), variance, kurtosis, skewness, harmonic mean, geometric 
151 
mean, mean, median, and bandwidth. These metrics provide insights into the distribution, central 
152 
tendency, and variability of the data [49]. The range of each variable was determined by subtracting 
153 
the minimum value from the maximum value, offering a fundamental understanding of data spread. 
154 
All metrics are presented in Table 3. 
155 
To assess multicollinearity among the independent variables time, temperature, pressure, and 
156 
co-solvent ratio, the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) was calculated for each predictor. VIF 
157 
quantifies the degree to which the variance of a regression coefficient is inflated due to linear 
158 
dependencies between variables [14]. As a general rule, VIF value exceeding 5 typically indicates 
159 
moderate multicollinearity, while values above 10 signal severe collinearity, necessitating 
160 
corrective measures such as variable removal or dimensionality reduction. 
161 
The predictive efficacy of five computational models was systematically evaluated for 
162 
estimating EO yields derived from SFE processes. These models included a hybrid convolutional 
163 
neural network-multilayer perceptron (CNN-MLP) architecture and four CNN-fed machine learning 
164 
methodologies: SVR, RF, GPR, and XGBoost. To approximate real-world generalization capability, 
165 
the dataset was partitioned using an 80:20 holdout validation protocol, which effectively prevented 
166 
data leakage between the training and testing subsets. Quantitative performance assessment was 
167 
conducted using six statistical indices: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), RMSE, Mean Squared Error 
168 
(MSE), Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient (r), Coefficient of Determination (R2), and Margin of 
169 
Deviation (MOD). These indices collectively capture error magnitude, linear association, explained 
170 
variance, and relative percentage deviations [17,18]. 
171 


6 
 
The statistical robustness of the predictions was rigorously examined using a two-tailed paired 
172 
Student’s t-test, with a significance threshold of α = 0.05. The null hypothesis (H0) posited that 
173 
there is no statistically significant difference between the means of the experimental and predicted 
174 
yield values. To further assess model consistency, a Bland–Altman analysis was conducted, in 
175 
which the discrepancies between predicted and observed yields were graphically plotted against 
176 
their respective means. The limits of agreement (LoA) were mathematically defined as the mean 
177 
bias ± 1.96 standard deviations of the differences, facilitating the identification of systematic biases 
178 
and anomalous outliers [50]. This dual-methodological framework, which integrates conventional 
179 
error metrics with bias-variance decomposition, ensured a comprehensive evaluation of predictive 
180 
reliability, thereby establishing a rigorous validation paradigm for industrial-scale SFE optimization 
181 
applications.

2.3. 
Machine and deep learning modeling techniques in cheminformatics 
187 
To address the dual complexity of plant-based cCO2 extraction, which stems from both the 
188 
molecular diversity of botanical matrices and the nonlinear behavior of process variables, a variety 
189 
of ML and DL models were employed for regression-based yield prediction. The primary objective 
190 
was to evaluate the capacity of these models to identify predictive relationships among chemical 
191 
structure, operational conditions, and extraction yield. 
192 
The chemical composition of each plant species was encoded using Morgan fingerprints 
193 
derived from the four most abundant bioactive compounds, as identified through literature-based 
194 
GC-MS profiles. Instead of relying on engineered descriptors, a CNN was employed to 
195 
automatically extract high level latent features from the 1024-bit fingerprint vectors. This approach 
196 
enabled the transformation of high-dimensional molecular data into compact, informative 
197 
representations that are suitable for integration with process parameters. 
198 
These CNN-derived molecular embeddings were concatenated with five normalized process 
199 
variables: temperature, pressure, extraction time, CO2 flow rate, and normalized co-solvent ratio, 
200 
and subsequently fed into a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for final yield prediction. The hybrid 
201 
CNN-MLP architecture was designed to jointly model the influence of chemical structure and 
202 
operational conditions, providing a unified, end-to-end predictive framework. 
203 
For benchmarking purposes, four classical ML regression models were trained using the same 
204 
input features: SVR, RF, GPR, and XGBoost. These widely adopted cheminformatics tools 
205 
provided robust baselines for comparative performance analysis. All models were evaluated using 
206 
an 80:20 train-test split, with hyperparameter optimization conducted through the OPTUNA 
207 
framework [51]. This standardized modeling pipeline ensured a fair and systematic comparison of 
208 
predictive accuracy across different architectures, highlighting the potential of deep hybrid models 
209 
in capturing complex extraction behaviors.

2.4. 
Hybrid CNN-MLP modeling framework 
212 
A hybrid DL architecture was developed to integrate molecular and process data for 
213 
predictive modeling of scCO2 extraction yields. The framework employed a two-layer CNN to 
214 
extract latent features from 1024-bit Morgan fingerprints, which were structured as 32×32 binary 
215 
matrices. Each convolutional layer was followed by a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation 
216 
function and a max-pooling operation, facilitating the hierarchical extraction of spatial patterns 
217 
within molecular structures. 
218 
To optimize feature encoding, the output from the final convolutional layer was flattened 
219 
into vectors of varying dimensions (4, 8, 32, and 64) during model tuning. The most informative 
220 


8 
 
feature embeddings were then concatenated with five normalized process variables to create a 
221 
hybrid input vector; the optimal architecture was presented in figure 3. This integrated feature set 
222 
was subsequently fed into a multilayer perceptron (MLP), which consisted of fully connected layers 
223 
trained using the Adam optimizer with a fixed learning rate of 0.001. Early stopping was 
224 
implemented with a patience of 10 epochs, up to a maximum of 3000 training epochs, to prevent 
225 
overfitting and enhance generalization.

3. 
Results and discussion 
265 
3.1. 
Statistical analysis of the dataset. 
266 
 
Before implementing ML models, a comprehensive statistical analysis was performed to 
267 
evaluate the structural integrity, distributional characteristics, and representativeness of the dataset. 
268 
Table 2 presents a comparative summary of the five input features: extraction time, temperature, 
269 
pressure, CO2 flow rate, normalized co-solvent ratio, and the target variable, extraction yield (% 
270 
w/w), across both training and testing subsets. This evaluation aimed to ensure consistency in data 
271 
distribution, identify potential challenges related to skewness or variability, and guide the selection 
272 
of suitable modeling strategies. 
273 
The extraction yield of EOs displayed a typical low-magnitude distribution, with the 
274 
majority of values concentrated below 5% w/w. This observation is consistent with the expected 
275 
behavior of volatile plant constituents, where the extracted compounds generally represent only a 
276 
small fraction of the original biomass [52]. The yield distribution was positively skewed, indicating 
277 
a predominance of low-yield outcomes, accompanied by a long tail of higher yields achieved under 
278 
optimized process settings or from particularly rich botanical sources. This asymmetry presents a 
279 
modeling challenge: algorithms must be capable of accurately capturing the frequent low-yield 
280 
cases while also recognizing the specific conditions that lead to high-yield exceptions. 
281 
Among all input variables, extraction time exhibited the greatest dispersion, ranging from 
282 
approximately 8 to 900 minutes, along with the highest degree of positive skewness. This wide 
283 
variation reflects differences in experimental designs across studies, which range from rapid 
284 
extractions targeting early-eluting volatiles to extended runs aimed at recovering less accessible 
285 
compounds. Such temporal variability underscores the necessity for models that can effectively 
286 
capture nonlinear relationships between extraction duration and yield dynamics. 
287 
Temperature and pressure distributions are relatively consistent across both subsets, with 
288 
mean values close to 50 °C and 20 MPa respectively, and moderate skewness. This alignment 
289 
supports consistency for the reliability of thermal and pressure-related factors. In contrast, the co-
290 
solvent ratio and flow rate exhibit high kurtosis and skewness in both subsets, with most data points 
291 
concentrated at lower values and a few extending cases pushing the upper range. For instance, the 
292 
flow rate in the training set ranges from 0.01 to 243.30 g/min (skewness = 5.96), while the testing 
293 
set spans from 0.02 to 243.30 g/min (skewness = 4.14), reflecting similar statistical behavior. These 
294 
patterns indicate that the model must be capable of capturing nonlinear relationships and be 
295 
sensitive to outliers. 
296 
The CO2 flow rate and normalized co-solvent ratio both demonstrated moderate to strong 
297 
positive skewness. Most experiments employed relatively low or no co-solvent volumes, which 
298 


11 
 
aligns with the principles of green chemistry that emphasize minimal use of organic modifiers. 
299 
However, the presence of a few high-intensity values indicates the potential for abrupt changes in 
300 
extraction efficiency, particularly when targeting polar compounds. These localized nonlinearities 
301 
require models with sufficient flexibility to identify and adapt to complex feature interactions. 
302

482

The extracted yield profiles reveal varying degrees of alignment between actual and 
485 
predicted yields across different plant species, each subjected to distinct operational conditions. For 
486

493

parameters and the chemical composition of the species.

Conclusion 
561 
This study successfully developed and validated a novel hybrid deep learning framework for 
562 
predicting supercritical CO2 extraction yields from various plant sources. By integrating molecular-
563 
level data with key process parameters, the proposed CNN-MLP model demonstrated exceptional 
564 
predictive power, achieving a high coefficient of determination (R2 = 0.974) and a low root mean 
565 
squared error (RMSE = 1.431) on the test set. Its performance significantly surpassed that of 
566 
traditional machine learning models, including RF, XGBoost, SVR, and GPR, establishing a new 
567 
benchmark for accuracy and reliability in this field. The model's robust performance, confirmed 
568 
through rigorous statistical validation methods, including paired t-tests and Bland-Altman analysis, 
569 
underscores its ability to navigate the complex, non-linear relationships inherent in the extraction 
570 
process. 
571 
The key innovation of this research lies in its dual-input architecture, which effectively 
572 
integrates chemical and engineering data. The CNN successfully distilled high-dimensional Morgan 
573 
fingerprints into compact, information-rich latent features, capturing the essential molecular 
574 


24 
 
properties relevant to extractability. When combined with process variables, the MLP was able to 
575 
model the synergistic effects between chemical structure and operational conditions. This integrated 
576 
approach proved essential for developing a generalized model capable of making accurate 
577 
predictions across a diverse dataset encompassing 21 different plant species and a wide range of 
578 
experimental settings. 
579 
Beyond its predictive accuracy, the practical utility of the CNN-MLP model was 
580 
demonstrated through rigorous external validation. When tested on an entirely unseen dataset for 
581 
Chamomilla recutita L. extraction, the model accurately reproduced time-resolved yield curves, 
582 
demonstrating its ability to generalize to new species and conditions not present in the initial 
583 
training data. This success in predicting kinetic profiles, rather than merely final yields, highlights 
584 
the model's potential for real-time process optimization. To facilitate its adoption, the optimized 
585 
model was deployed as an interactive web application, providing a seamless and accessible tool for 
586 
researchers to obtain instant yield predictions without requiring expertise in machine learning. 
587 
While the proposed framework represents a significant advancement, this study also 
588 
identified areas for future improvement. The model occasionally underpredicted yields during late-
589 
stage extractions, indicating that its understanding of mass transfer limitations could be enhanced. 
590 
Future research should focus on incorporating additional physicochemical descriptors related to 
591 
plant matrix properties, such as particle size, porosity, and mass transfer coefficients. Integrating 
592 
this domain knowledge, potentially through physics-informed machine learning approaches, would 
593 
further bridge the gap between data-driven predictions and mechanistic understanding. Such 
594 
refinements will be crucial for developing scalable and highly reliable models that can accelerate 
595 
the optimization and industrial application of SFE.

Abstract: 37 The efficient extraction of essential oils (EOs), particularly volatile compounds, from medicinal, 38 aromatic, or oil-rich crop plants using supercritical carbon dioxide extraction (scCO2) is crucial for 39 industries such as pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and food. However, optimizing this process presents 40 challenges due to the intricate molecular diversity of the compounds and the complex interplay of 41 scCO2 parameters. To address these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid predictive framework 42 that combines deep learning and machine learning, utilizing 694 scCO2 experimental data points 43 sourced from the literature across 21 plant species. Four major molecular compounds per plant were 44 selected as input features, alongside key process parameters, including temperature, pressure, 45 extraction time, co-solvent ratio, and CO2 flow rate. Morgan fingerprints were computed for these 46 compounds, and a convolutional neural network (CNN) was utilized to extract their high-level 47 representations into compact vectors. These vectors were integrated with normalized process 48 parameters and fed into a CNN-Multilayer Perceptron (CNN-MLP) hybrid architecture. 49 Performance was compared with Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest (RF), Gaussian 50 Process Regression (GPR), and XGBoost, all optimized using OPTUNA. The CNN-MLP achieved 51 the best performance, with an R2 of 0.974 and a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 1.431 on the 52 test set. A paired t-test (p = 0.810) and Bland–Altman analysis (mean difference: 9.35%) confirmed 53 the model's robustness. To further assess generalizability, external validations were conducted using 54 unseen experimental conditions. The CNN-MLP was tested on three extraction profiles and 55 demonstrated strong predictive performance, with Pearson correlations ranging from 0.95 to 0.98. 56
